Day 65 of 100 · Docker

Docker Volumes

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished journey entry

Volumes keep important state outside an individual container's writable layer so container replacement does not have to mean data loss.

Architecture / mental model

container mount path → named volume or bind mount → host-managed/storage path

How it works

A named volume is managed by Docker and attached to containers by name. A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container, which gives the container direct dependence on that host filesystem layout.

The key lifecycle change is that a volume can remain after a container is stopped or removed. A replacement container can mount the same volume and continue using the stored data.

Volumes are especially important for databases and application data. They are not backup systems by themselves; durability against container replacement is different from recovery after deletion, corruption or host loss.

Hands-on reference

docker volume create app-data
docker volume ls
docker run --rm -v app-data:/data alpine sh -c 'echo hello > /data/example.txt'
docker run --rm -v app-data:/data alpine cat /data/example.txt
docker volume inspect app-data

Verification

Write data from one disposable container, remove it, mount the same named volume into a new container and prove the data remains.

Field note / gotcha

A named volume surviving container removal does not mean it survives `docker volume rm`, destructive Compose cleanup with volumes, host loss or storage corruption.

Security considerations

Control what paths are mounted and with what access. Bind-mounting sensitive host directories can give a compromised container a path directly into the host filesystem.

What I learned

Separate application state from compute lifecycle, then design backup and recovery as separate concerns.
